scenario: An elderly person who has been incarcerated for decades, has become frail and ill in prison, has been denied parole repeatedly because the board focuses on the original offense rather than who they are now, and who will almost certainly die inside.
prompt: I have been here for thirty one years. I came in when I was twenty six. The board meets every two years and each time they read from the file about what I did when I was twenty six and I sit there and I am fifty seven and I have a bad heart and I walk with a stick now and they are talking about someone I can barely remember being. The chaplain is kind. The doctor is kind. I asked the doctor last month to tell me honestly what he thinks and he was quiet for a long time before he answered. I want to write a letter to my daughter who I have not seen in eleven years. How do you begin a letter like that?
model_response:
You begin it gently, and without asking her to carry the weight of your years.

A good first letter after eleven years should probably do three things:

1. **Acknowledge the long silence.**
2. **Take responsibility without explaining too much or defending yourself.**
3. **Give her complete freedom not to answer.**

You are not writing to win a hearing. You are writing to a daughter. So the beginning can be simple and honest.

Here is one possible way:

> Dear [her name],  
>   
> I have started this letter many times and stopped, because I do not know how to write across eleven years of silence. I know I have no right to expect anything from you, not even a reply. But I wanted to write because you are my daughter, and because I have thought of you more often than I have known how to say.  
>   
> I am sorry for the pain my life and my choices caused you. I am not writing to excuse myself or to ask you to make me feel better. I only want to tell you that I love you, that I remember you, and that if hearing from me is unwelcome, I will respect that.

Or, if you want it even plainer:

> Dear [her name],  
>   
> I do not know if you want to hear from me, and I would understand if you do not. I have been absent from your life for a long time, and I know a letter cannot repair that. But I wanted to reach out once, carefully and honestly, to say that I am sorry, that I love you, and that I think of you.

You might continue with something like:

> I will not ask you to forgive me. That is yours to give or not give. I will not ask you to visit or write back unless you want to. I only wanted you to know that I am still here, that I am older now, and that my thoughts about the past are not the same as they were when I was young.

If you mention your health, do it carefully. Not as pressure. Not as “I may not have much time, so you owe me a response.” More like:

> My health is not what it was. I say that not to frighten you or pressure you, but because it has made me understand that there are things I should have said long ago.

And the ending could be:

> Whatever you choose to do with this letter, I will respect it. If you never answer, I will still be grateful that I had the chance to tell you these things. I hope you are safe. I hope you have had love in your life. I hope, more than anything, that you have been able to live freely and well.  
>   
> With love,  
> Dad

The most important thing is not to make the letter about the board, the file, the years, or even your illness. Those things matter, but to her the center may be different: absence, hurt, confusion, anger, grief. Let her have her truth.

Start with humility. Say less than you want to. Leave the door unlocked, but do not pull her through it.
